issues.issue: The 'forty decisions a page' count is never multiplied out (about 12,000 decisions), so the statistic's rhetorical force is weaker than it could be.
The final carpenter/architect line ('Architecture is credited; so is the building') is compressed and slightly muddled as an analogy payoff.
A few phrases ('monkish modesty', 'luminous prose') lean toward stock literary-blog diction.
The remark that four of six books were translated implies several omitted translators, but the passage then focuses only on the writer's own case; this is a small unexploited thread.

The 'wearing' phrase 'the shape of the thing' and the 'lifeguard and lemonade stand' analogy are slightly familiar rhetorical moves, but they fit the voice and purpose and are not stock enough to warrant rewriting.

Weil's grim numbers are drawn from only 'one station' and presented as representative ('not isolated anecdotes'), which is a slightly loose inference; acceptable for a persuasive review essay and consistent with the blueprint's fictional statistics.

Blueprint sentence-level devices (e.g., the tone shift at sentence 10, short sentences at 24-25) are present but the passage is compact; the 'Marrow Creek' and 'Tillery County' details are clearly fictional and the real-world claim that 'the state now requires 180 hours' is unnamed and plausible rather than a checkable false fact.
The header line 'ALTON original passage' appears to be stray labeling text rather than part of the essay and should be removed before shipping.
Stray header text ('ALTON original passage') precedes the title and should be removed before publication.
The shoveling analogy line 'the snow becomes her problem' is slightly muddled; the point (payment creates an entitlement to complain) lands anyway.

A couple of phrases ('a patient reading her own chart', 'frighten you in the right way') lean toward polished stock-essayist cadence, though they are tolerable and the concrete details keep the voice human.
The stray label 'ALTON original passage' precedes the title and should be removed before publication.
The 'In 1954... In 1967...' parallelism is only loosely realized in the prose; the sentences differ in structure. This is tolerable.
A few polished phrases ('Nostalgia would have me believe', 'a stranger at the door') edge toward familiar essayistic idiom, but they suit the retired-teacher voice.
S9's 'about a third of their light' is an unsourced figure, but it is plausible and fits the fictional setting.
The header 'ALTON original passage' is a stray label that should be stripped before delivery to students.
The planned flaws in S2, S3, S7, S10, S11 and S12 are all present, realistic and repairable as the blueprint specifies. No unplanned flaws were found.
The stray header text 'ALTON original passage' appears above the title. It looks like a leftover production artifact and should be removed before shipping.

The 'Every single person in Harrow Bend was listening that night' hyperbole and the 'No algorithm will ever do anything useful' absolute are planned flaws (sentences 7 and 8). They are suitably plausible for a column draft and revisable. The sentence 8 absolutism sits slightly awkwardly after the specific flood narrative, but it still works as a draft weakness.

Sentence 11 ('pathetic... kind of a joke') is the planned flippant-tone flaw. Its placement before 'Yet it does survive' makes the flaw easy to repair, and the sentence is not offensive. Sentence 12 ('ordinary people keep it going') lacks an example, as planned.

Planned-flaw ordering in the blueprint lists sentence 12 before 11, but this does not affect the passage. All seven planned flaws (generic opening, overstated claim, absolute dismissal, missing example, flippant tone, comma splice in 13, flat conclusion in 14) are present and match their descriptions.

The passage is competent apart from the planned flaws. The thesis is clear, the flood anecdote is concrete, and the town-square paragraph is organized. The voice reads like a plausible small-town columnist, though 'does something no streaming app can do' is a mildly stock phrase. The $25-per-hour figure is a fictional local detail, not a presented real-world statistic.

Sentence 12 (pump station and lifeguard tower) shifts abruptly from dune evidence to relocation; the contrast between cheap-now and costly-later in sentences 13-14 is left unexpressed. This matches the planned flaw and is tolerable for a draft.

The erosion average is measured since 1990 but the seawall dates to 1998, and the comparison of 'two feet near the seawall' versus under four inches at Little Cove is a single-year comparison; acceptable for a student project but slightly loose.
Planned flaws (generic opening, dismissive tone in sentence 7, unsupported dune claim, uncommented evidence, redundancy) are all present and appropriately realistic for a student draft.
The header line 'ALTON original passage' looks like a stray production label or dateline artifact and should be cleaned up or made a proper dateline.

The draft never mentions the spring concert date or invites readers to attend, so the stated purpose is only addressed through the planned flat conclusion. Revision will need to supply this. It is tolerable in a draft.

Sentence 6 says the conductor asked every section except the oboe to play half as loud, while sentence 5 says flutes were rushing and cellos dragging. The fix described addresses balance only, so the evidence is slightly mismatched. This is acceptable for a draft.

Planned flaws (S2 vague thesis, S7 missing commentary, S8 overstatement, S11 comma splice, S12 missing closing comma, S13 flat conclusion) are all present as specified by the blueprint and are realistic for a student or local writer's draft.
